371.subject: Botany
371.text: Which of the following helps in ascent of sap?
371.sol: Water is mainly absorbed by roots which goes upwards so as to replace water loss in transpiration and to be used in photosynthesis. This upward movement of water from roots to leaves through stem against force of gravity is called ascent of sap. Different theories have been put forward in support of ascent of sap. They include root pressure theory, capillary theory and transpiration pull theory. Root pressure is developed when rate of absorption is more than rate of transpiration and so water is pushed up in the tracheary elements. Capillary force theory was given by Bohm, according to which xylem vessels act as minute capillaries and water rises in these capillaries due to capillary action or surface tension. According to transpiration pull theory by Dixon and Jolly, due to water loss by transpiration suction pressure is increased and water is absorbed from adjacent xylem vessels of leaves and thus sap in under tension.

1923.subject: Zoology
1923.text: In a standard ECG which one of the following alphabets is the correct representation of the respective activity of the human heart?
1923.sol: A normal electrogram (ECG) is composed of a P wave, a QRS wave (complex) and a $\mathrm{T}$ wave. The P-wave represents the electrical excitation or depolarisation of the atria. The QRS complex represents the depolarisation of the ventricles which initiates the ventricular contraction. The contraction starts shortly after Q and marks the beginning of the systole. The T-wave represents the repolarisation of ventricles. The end of the T-wave marks the end of systole.

4833.subject: Chemistry
4833.text: How many of the following polymers given, come under the category of condensation polymers? Bakelite, Teflon, Nylon-6, Dacron, Polyisoprene, Melamine, Neoprene
4833.sol:
The given polymers are formed as follows : Bakelite These are made by the condensation reaction of formaldehyde and phenol in presence of either an acid or base, as a catalyst. It involves the formation of methylene bridges in ortho/ para position.
On heating with formaldehyde, novolac undergoes cross-linking to form an infusible solid mass, which is known as bakelite.
It is a condensation polymer. Teflon It is prepared by heating tetrafluoroethylene at high pressure in the presence of peroxides or ammonium peroxo sulphate $\left[ \left(\mathrm{NH}_4\right)_2 \mathrm{ S}_2 \mathrm{O}_8\right] catalyst. It is chemically inert$ and $resistant to attack.
It is an addition polymer. Nylon-6 or Perlon It is also known as perlon and is obtained from the monomer caprolactum. This caprolactum is obtained from cyclohexane.
Here, in both monomeric species, there are 6 carbon atoms each. Dacron or Terylene It is a polymer obtained by condensation reaction between ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid at 425-475 \mathrm{ K}$ in the presence of zinc acetate antimony trioxide catalyst.
Nylon-6 and dacron both are condensation polymers. Polyisoprene
It also an addition polymer. Melamine In this particular reaction, melamine and formaldehyde copolymerise to give another polymer
Thus, is a condensation polymer. Neoprene It is also called polychloroprene and formed by the free radial polymerisation of chloroprene and has superior resistance to vegetable and mineral oils.
It is an addition polymer. Hence, among the given polymers, we have four (4) condensation-polymers and option (a) is the correct answer.

12138.text: Let& $a, b$ and $c$ be distinct and none of them is equal to $1$. If the lines $x + ay + a = 0 bx + y + b = 0$ and $cx + cy + 1 = 0$ are concurrent, then the value of $\dfrac{a}{a - 1} + \dfrac{b}{b - 1} + \dfrac{c}{c - 1}$ is
12138.sol:
We know that, three lines

${a}_{1}x + {b}_{1}y + {c}_{1} = 0$

${a}_{2}x + {b}_{2}y + {c}_{2} = 0$

${a}_{3}x + {b}_{3}y + {c}_{3} = 0$

are concurrent if

$\left|\begin{cases}{a}_{1} & {b}_{1} & {c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{2} \\ {a}_{3} & {b}_{3} & {c}_{3}\end{cases}\right| = 0$

Therefore, given lines are concurrent if

$\left|\begin{cases}1 & a & a \\ b & 1 & b \\ c & c & 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

Expanding along ${R}_{1}$, we have

$1\left(1 - bc\right) - a \left(b - bc\right) + a \left($ bc - c\right) = 0$

or $ab + bc + ca = 1 + 2abc . . . $\left($ i\right)$

Now,

\dfrac{a}{a - 1} + \dfrac{b}{b - 1} + \dfrac{c}{c - 1}$

$= \dfrac{a\left(b - 1\right)\left(c - 1\right) + b\left(a - 1\right)\left(c - 1\right) + c\left(a - 1\right)\left(b - 1\right)}{\left(a - 1\right)\left(b - 1\right)\left(c - 1\right)}$

$= \dfrac{3abc + \left(a + b + c\right) - 2\left(ab + bc + ca\right)}{1 - \left(a + b + c\right) + \left($ ab + bc + ca\right) - abc}$

Substituting the value of $ab + bc + ca$ from& \left($ i\right)$, we get

\dfrac{3abc + \left(a + b + c\right) - 2 - 4abc}{1 - \left(a + b + c\right) + 1 + 2abc - abc}$

$= \dfrac{- abc + \left(a + b + c\right) - 2}{2 - \left(a + b + c\right) + abc}$

$= - \left(\${\dfrac{abc - \left(a + b + c\right) + 2}{abc - \left(a + b + c\right) + 2}\right\}

$= - 1$

16512.text: An iron sphere having diameter $D$ and mass $M$ is immersed in hot water so that the temperature of the sphere increases by $\delta T$. If $\alpha$ is the coefficient of linear expansion of the iron then the change in the surface area of the sphere is

Initial surface area, $A=4 \pi R^2=4 \pi\left(\frac{D}{2}\right)^2=\pi D^2$...(i)
Surface area after heating by temperature $\delta T$,
$A^{\prime}=4 \pi\left(\frac{D^{\prime}}{2}\right)^2=\pi\left(D^{\prime}\right)^2$...(ii)
where $D^{\prime}$ is the new diameter.
From the equation of linear expansion, we have
$D^{\prime}=D(1+\alpha \delta T)$...(iii)
putting the value of $D^{\prime}$ from eq. (iii) in eq. (ii) we get
$A^{\prime}=\pi D^2(1+\alpha \delta T)^2=\pi D^2  \lleft(1+\alpha^$2 \deltaT^2+$2 \alpha \deltaT\right)...(iv)
\begin{aligned} & =\$piD^2\lleft(1+\alpha^$2 \deltaT^2+$2 \alpha \deltaT\right)-\piD^$2\\ & =\$piD^2\lleft[1+\alpha^$2 \deltaT^2+$2 \alpha \deltaT-1\right] \\ & =\$piD^2\left[\alpha^2 \deltaT^2+$2 $\alpha \deltaT\right]\end{aligned}
Change$ in surface area=A^{\prime}-A \doteq \piD^{\prime 2}-\piD^2=\piD^2$\alpha \deltaT(\alpha. \deltaT+$2)$

16691.text: In a Carnot's engine if the temperatures of the source and the sink are decreased by $100 \mathrm{ K}$ each then the efficiency of the engine
16691.sol:
Initial efficiency is given by
$\eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\frac{T_1-T_2}{T_1}$
Decreased by $100 \mathrm{ K}$ each the efficiency
$\begin{aligned} & \eta=1-\frac{T_2-100}{T_1-100} \\ & =\frac{T_1-100-T_2+100}{T_1-100}=\frac{T_1-T_2}{T_1-100}\end{aligned}$

16935.text: Young's double slit experiment is conducted with monochromatic light of wavelength $5000 Å$, with slit separation of $3 \mathrm{ mm}$ and observer at $20 \mathrm{ cm}$ away from the slits. 16935.sol:
Given, wavelength, $\lambda=5000 Å=5 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{ m}$
Slit separation, $d=3 \mathrm{ mm}=3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{ m}$ Distance between slit and screen,
$D=20 \mathrm{ cm}=0.2 \mathrm{ m}$
Thickness of transparent plate $=1 \mathrm{ mm}=1 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{ m}$
Fringe shift, $\Delta x=6 \mathrm{ mm}=6 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{ m}$
Fringe shift' is given by
$\Delta x=\frac{D}{d}(\mu-1) t\Rightarrow \quad 6 \times 10^{-3}=\frac{0.2}{3 \times 10^{-3}}(\mu-1) \times 10^{-3}\Rightarrow \frac{6 \times 3 \times 10^{-3}}{0.2}=\mu-1 \Rightarrow 9 \times 10^{-2}=\mu-1\Rightarrow \quad \mu=1.09$
Hence, refractive index of transparent plate is 1.09.

19033.text: A ball of mass $0.2 \mathrm{~kg}$ is thrown vertically upwards by applying a force by hand. 19033.sol: Let the velocity of the ball just when it leaves the hand is $u$ then applying, $$\begin{array}{l} v^{2}-u^{2}=2 a $\text{$ for upward journey } \\ \Rightarrow-u^{2}=2(-10) \times 2 \\ \Rightarrow u^{2}=40 \end{array}$ Again applying $v^{2}-u^{2}=2 a s$ for the upward journey of the ball, when the ball is in the hands of the thrower, $\begin{array}{l}v^{2}-u^{2}=2 a s \\ \Rightarrow 40-0=2(a) 0.2 \\ \Rightarrow a=100 $\mathrm{~m}$/ \mathrms^{2} \\ \therefore $\mathrm{F}=$m a=0.2 \times100=20 $\mathrm{~N}$\\ \Rightarrow $\mathrm{N}-$m g=20 \\ \Rightarrow $\mathrm{N}=$20+2=22 $\mathrm{~N}$ \end{array}

19476.subject: Chemistry
19476.text: A compound [X] undergoes reactions as given. Identify compounds [C] and [D] formed in these reactions.
19476.sol:
The given starting compound is isopropyl phenyl ether, $Ph-O-CH(CH_3)_2$.

Reaction with concentrated HI leads to the cleavage of the ether. Due to the partial double bond character of the O-phenyl bond (arising from resonance), the cleavage occurs at the O-isopropyl bond. This yields phenol and isopropyl iodide.
$Ph-O-CH(CH_3)_2 + HI \rightarrow PhOH + CH_3-CH(I)-CH_3$
Since [A] is the aromatic product, [A] is Phenol and [B] is Isopropyl iodide.

Phenol [A] undergoes oxidation with acidified dichromate (Cr_2O_7^{2-} / H^+$) to form p-benzoquinone.
Therefore, [C] is Benzoquinone.

Isopropyl iodide [B] reacts with aqueous KOH to undergo nucleophilic substitution, forming isopropyl alcohol.
$CH_3-CH(I)-CH_3 + aq. KOH \rightarrow CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3$

Isopropyl alcohol contains the $CH_3-CH(OH)-$ group, which gives a positive iodoform test when treated with $I_2$ and a base like $Na_2CO_3$. The reaction produces iodoform and the sodium salt of the corresponding carboxylic acid (sodium acetate).
$CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3 + I_2 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow CHI_3 + CH_3COONa$
Therefore, [D] is Iodoform.

Answer: [C]: Benzoquinone [D]: Iodoform$

19752.subject: Chemistry
19752.text: Which one of the following molecules attains greater stability on formation of its diatomic monovalent anion?
19752.sol: The stability of a molecule upon the formation of its diatomic monovalent anion depends on the change in bond order. The bond order is calculated as $\dfrac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)$, where $N_b$ is the number of bonding electrons and $N_a$ is the number of antibonding electrons. For $\mathrm{C}_2$, the configuration is $\sigma_{1s}^{2} \sigma_{1s}^{*2} \sigma_{2s}^{2} \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \pi_{2p_x}^{2} \pi_{2p_y}^{2}$. Bond order = $\dfrac{1}{2}(8 - 4) = 2$. Adding an electron gives $\mathrm{C}_2^{-}$, configuration $\sigma_{1s}^{2} \sigma_{1s}^{*2} \sigma_{2s}^{2} \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \pi_{2p_x}^{2} \pi_{2p_y}^{2} \sigma_{2p_z}^{1}$. Bond order = $\dfrac{1}{2}(9 - 4) = 2.5$. Since the bond order increases, stability increases. For $\mathrm{F}_2$, the configuration is $\sigma_{1s}^{2} \sigma_{1s}^{*2} \sigma_{2s}^{2} \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \sigma_{2p_z}^{2} \pi_{2p_x}^{2} \pi_{2p_y}^{2} \pi_{2p_x}^{*2} \pi_{2p_y}^{*2}$. Bond order = $\dfrac{1}{2}(10 - 8) = 1$. Adding an electron gives $\mathrm{F}_2^{-}$, configuration $\dots \pi_{2p_x}^{*2} \pi_{2p_y}^{*2} \sigma_{2p_z}^{*1}$. Bond order = $\dfrac{1}{2}(10 - 9) = 0.5$. Stability decreases. For $\mathrm{O}_2$, the configuration is $\sigma_{1s}^{2} \sigma_{1s}^{*2} \sigma_{2s}^{2} \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \sigma_{2p_z}^{2} \pi_{2p_x}^{2} \pi_{2p_y}^{2} \pi_{2p_x}^{*1} \pi_{2p_y}^{*1}$. Bond order = $\dfrac{1}{2}(10 - 6) = 2$. Adding an electron gives $\mathrm{O}_2^{-}$, configuration $\dots \pi_{2p_x}^{*2} \pi_{2p_y}^{*1}$. Bond order = $\dfrac{1}{2}(10 - 7) = 1.5$. Stability decreases. For $\mathrm{N}_2$, the configuration is $\sigma_{1s}^{2} \sigma_{1s}^{*2} \sigma_{2s}^{2} \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \pi_{2p_x}^{2} \pi_{2p_y}^{2} \sigma_{2p_z}^{2}$. Bond order = $\dfrac{1}{2}(10 - 4) = 3$. Adding an electron gives $\mathrm{N}_2^{-}$, configuration $\dots \sigma_{2p_z}^{2} \pi_{2p_x}^{*1}$. Bond order = $\dfrac{1}{2}(10 - 5) = 2.5$. Stability decreases. Thus, $\mathrm{C}_2$ is the only molecule where the bond order increases upon forming the anion, leading to greater stability. Answer: $\mathrm{C}_2$

19964.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
19964.text:
Which of the following statements is/are true about the diagonal relationship of Be and Al ?
(i) Both react with NaOH to liberate hydrogen.
(ii) Their oxides are basic.
(iii) They are made passive by nitric acid.
(iv) Their carbides give acetylene on treatment with water.
19964.sol:
Statement given in (i) and (iii) are correct, while in (ii) and (iv) are incorrect.
BeO and $\mathrm{Al}_2 \mathrm{O}_3$ are amphoteric. These react with acid as well as alkalines to given corresponding salts.
$\begin{aligned} \\ & \mathrm{BeO}+2 \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{BeCl}_2+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \\ \\ & \mathrm{BeO}+2 \mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}_2 \mathrm{BeO}_2+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \\ \\ & \mathrm{Al}_2 \mathrm{O}_3+6 \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{AlCl}_3+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \\ \\ & \mathrm{Al}_2 \mathrm{O}_3+2 \mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{NaAlO}_2+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \\ \end{aligned}$
$\mathrm{Be}_2 \mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{Al}_4 \mathrm{C}_3$ give methane on treatment with water.
$\begin{aligned} \\ & \mathrm{Be}_2 \mathrm{C}+4 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_2+\mathrm{CH}_4 \\ \\ & \mathrm{Al}_4 \mathrm{C}_3+12 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \longrightarrow 4 \mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{OH})_3+3 \mathrm{CH}_4 \\ \end{aligned}$

21217.subject: Mathematics
21217.text: The function $y = ||x| - 1|$ is differentiable for all values of '$x$' except
21217.sol:
The given function is $y = ||x| - 1|$.

A function of the form $|f(x)|$ is generally non-differentiable at points where $f(x) = 0$ (if the curve crosses the x-axis) and at points where $f(x)$ itself is non-differentiable.

First, the inner function $f(x) = |x| - 1$ involves $|x|$, which is non-differentiable at $x = 0$.
For $x$ in the neighborhood of $0$ (i.e., $-1 < x < 1$), $y = ||x| - 1| = 1 - |x|$.
The left-hand derivative at $x = 0$ is $1$ and the right-hand derivative is $-1$. Thus, $y$ is non-differentiable at $x = 0$.

Second, we check where the expression inside the outer modulus becomes zero:
$|x| - 1 = 0$
$\Rightarrow |x| = 1$
$\Rightarrow x = 1$ or $x = -1$

At $x = 1$, for $x > 1$, $y = x - 1$ (derivative is $1$). For $0 < x < 1$, $y = 1 - x$ (derivative is $-1$). Thus, $y$ is non-differentiable at $x = 1$.

At $x = -1$, for $x < -1$, $y = -x - 1$ (derivative is $-1$). For $-1 < x < 0$, $y = x + 1$ (derivative is $1$). Thus, $y$ is non-differentiable at $x = -1$.

Therefore, the function is differentiable for all values of $x$ except at $x \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$.

Answer: $\{-1 , 0 , 1\}$

22266.subject: Mathematics
22266.text: $The expression \dfrac{\tan A}{1-\cot A}+\dfrac{\cot A}{1-\tan A}$ can be written as
22266.sol:
Let the expression be $E = \dfrac{\tan A}{1-\cot A} + \dfrac{\cot A}{1-\tan A}$.

Substituting $\cot A = \dfrac{1}{\tan A}$ into the expression:

$E = \dfrac{\tan A}{1-\dfrac{1}{\tan A}} + \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{\tan A}}{1-\tan A}$

$E = \dfrac{\tan^2 A}{\tan A - 1} + \dfrac{1}{\tan A(1-\tan A)}$

$E = \dfrac{\tan^2 A}{\tan A - 1} - \dfrac{1}{\tan A(\tan A - 1)}$

$E = \dfrac{\tan^3 A - 1}{\tan A(\tan A - 1)}$

Using the identity $a^3 - b^3 = (a-b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)$ where $a = \tan A$ and $b = 1$:

$E = \dfrac{(\tan A - 1)(\tan^2 A + \tan A + 1)}{\tan A(\tan A - 1)}$

$E = \dfrac{\tan^2 A + \tan A + 1}{\tan A}$

$E = \tan A + 1 + \cot A$

$E = 1 + \dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A} + \dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A}$

$E = 1 + \dfrac{\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A}{\sin A \cos A}$

$E = 1 + \dfrac{1}{\sin A \cos A}$

$E = 1 + \sec A \operatorname{cosec} A$.

Answer: $\sec A \operatorname{cosec} A+1$

22443.subject: Physics
22443.text: In the head-on collision of two alpha particles $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ with the gold nucleus, the closest approaches are 31.4 fermi and 94.2 fermi respectively. Then the ratio of the energy possessed by the alpha particles $\alpha_2 / \alpha_1$ is:
22443.sol:
The distance of closest approach $r_0$ for an alpha particle of kinetic energy $K$ colliding head-on with a nucleus of atomic number $Z$ is given by the formula $r_0 = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{2Ze^2}{K}$.

From this expression, it is evident that $r_0 \propto \dfrac{1}{K}$, which implies $K \propto \dfrac{1}{r_0}$.

Given the closest approaches for the two alpha particles are $r_1 = 31.4$ fermi and $r_2 = 94.2$ fermi, the ratio of their kinetic energies $K_2 / K_1$ is given by:

$\dfrac{K_2}{K_1} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2}$

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{K_2}{K_1} = \dfrac{31.4}{94.2} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Answer: $1: 3$

23266.subject: Physics
23266.text: Select the correct statement from the following:
options: Nuclear force is the weakest force in nature
Nuclear force is a non central force
Nuclear force depends on the charge of the nucleons
Nuclear force is a long range force
23266.sol:
Nuclear forces are the strongest forces in nature, acting between nucleons within the nucleus. They are short-range forces, effective only up to distances of the order of $10^{-15}$ m (femtometers).

Nuclear forces are charge-independent, meaning they act equally between proton-proton, neutron-neutron, and proton-neutron pairs, provided the distance is the same.

Nuclear forces are non-central forces, as they do not act only along the line joining the centers of the two nucleons; they depend on the spin and orientation of the nucleons.

Answer: Nuclear force is a non central force

23534.subject: Physics
23534.text: Two black bodies $\mathrm{P}$ and $\mathrm{Q}$ have equal surface areas and are kept at temperatures $127^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ and $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ respectively. The ratio of thermal power radiated by A to that by B is
23534.sol:
The thermal power radiated by a black body is given by the Stefan-Boltzmann law: $P = \sigma A T^{4}$, where $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $A$ is the surface area, and $T$ is the absolute temperature in Kelvin.

Given the temperatures in Celsius:
$T_{P} = 127^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C} = 127 + 273 = 400 \text{ K}$
$T_{Q} = 27^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C} = 27 + 273 = 300 \text{ K}$

The ratio of thermal power radiated by P to that by Q is:
$\dfrac{P_{P}}{P_{Q}} = \dfrac{\sigma A T_P^{4}}{\sigma A T_Q^{4}} = \left( \dfrac{T_{P}}{T_{Q}} \right)^{4}$

Substituting the values:
$\dfrac{P_{P}}{P_{Q}} = \left( \dfrac{400}{300} \right)^{4} = \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right)^{4}$

Calculating the power:
$\dfrac{P_{P}}{P_{Q}} = \dfrac{4^{4}}{3^{4}} = \dfrac{256}{81}$

Answer: $256: 81$

25527.subject: Mathematics
25527.text:
Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of all positive integers. Consider the sets
$A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ and $B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}$.
Let $S$ be the set of all functions $f: A \rightarrow B$ such that $f(2) \neq 2$ and $f(4) \neq 4$. Consider the set
$T = \{f \in S : \text{there exists a function } g : B \rightarrow \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } g(f(x)) = 2^x \text{ for all } x \in A\}$.
Then the number of elements in the set $T$ is ___________.
25527.sol:
The condition $g(f(x)) = 2^x$ for all $x \in A$ implies that if $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$, then $g(f(x_1)) = g(f(x_2))$, which gives $2^{x_1} = 2^{x_2} \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2$.

Thus, $f$ must be an injective (one-to-one) function. Conversely, if $f$ is injective, such a function $g$ can always be constructed. Therefore, $T$ is the set of all injective functions $f: A ightarrow B$ such that $f(2) eq 2$ and $f(4) eq 4$.

The total number of injective functions from $A$ to $B$ is $^{7}P_{5} = 7 imes 6 imes 5 imes 4 imes 3 = 2520$.

Let $E_2$ be the set of injective functions where $f(2) = 2$. The number of such functions is $^{6}P_{4} = 6 imes 5 imes 4 imes 3 = 360$.

Let $E_4$ be the set of injective functions where $f(4) = 4$. The number of such functions is $^{6}P_{4} = 360$.

Let $E_2 \cap E_4$ be the set of injective functions where both $f(2) = 2$ and $f(4) = 4$. The number of such functions is $^{5}P_{3} = 5 imes 4 imes 3 = 60$.

Using the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion, the number of injective functions where $f(2) = 2$ or $f(4) = 4$ is:

$|E_2 \cup E_4| = |E_2| + |E_4| - |E_2 \cap E_4| = 360 + 360 - 60 = 660$

The number of elements in the set $T$ is the number of injective functions where $f(2) eq 2$ and $f(4) eq 4$, which is:

$|T| = 2520 - 660 = 1860$

Answer: $1860$

25924.text:
Match each entry in List-I to the correct entry in List-II and choose the correct option.
List-IList-II
(P) The number of elements in the set $\{x \in [-\pi, \pi] : \sin^6 x + \cos^4 x = 1\}$(1) is $1$
(Q) The number of elements in the set $\left\{x \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] : \sin^2 x + \cos^6 x = 1\right\}$(2) is $2$
(R) The number of elements in the set $\left\{x \in [-\pi, \pi] : \cos^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - \sin^2 x = \dfrac{1}{2}\right\}$(3) is $3$
(S) The number of elements in the set $\left\{x \in [-2\pi, 2\pi] : 6\sin^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - \cos 3x = 3\right\}$(4) is $4$
(5) is $5$
25924.sol:
For (P):
$\sin^6 x + \cos^4 x = 1$
$\sin^6 x + (1 - \sin^2 x)^2 = 1$
$\sin^6 x + 1 - 2\sin^2 x + \sin^4 x = 1$
$\sin^2 x (\sin^4 x + \sin^2 x - 2) = 0$
$\sin^2 x (\sin^2 x - 1)(\sin^2 x + 2) = 0$
This gives $\sin^2 x = 0$ or $\sin^2 x = 1$.
In the interval $[-\pi, \pi]$, the solutions are $x \in \{-\pi, -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\}$.
Number of solutions = $5$.

For (Q):
$\sin^2 x + \cos^6 x = 1$
$1 - \cos^2 x + \cos^6 x = 1$
$\cos^2 x (\cos^4 x - 1) = 0$
This gives $\cos^2 x = 0$ or $\cos^2 x = 1$.
In the interval $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, the solutions are $x \in \left\{-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\}$.
Number of solutions = $3$.

For (R):
$\cos^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - \sin^2 x = \dfrac{1}{2}$
$\dfrac{1 + \cos x}{2} - (1 - \cos^2 x) = \dfrac{1}{2}$
$1 + \cos x - 2 + 2\cos^2 x = 1$
$2\cos^2 x + \cos x - 2 = 0$
Solving the quadratic equation for $\cos x$, we get:
$\cos x = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{17}}{4}$
Since $\cos x \in [-1, 1]$, we reject the negative root. Thus, $\cos x = \dfrac{\sqrt{17} - 1}{4}$.
Since $0 < \dfrac{\sqrt{17} - 1}{4} < 1$, there are exactly $2$ solutions in $[-\pi, \pi]$.
Number of solutions = $2$.

For (S):
$6\sin^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) - \cos 3x = 3$
$3(1 - \cos x) - (4\cos^3 x - 3\cos x) = 3$
$3 - 3\cos x - 4\cos^3 x + 3\cos x = 3$
$-4\cos^3 x = 0 \Rightarrow \cos x = 0$
In the interval $[-2\pi, 2\pi]$, the solutions are $x \in \left\{-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}, -\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right\}$.
Number of solutions = $4$.

Therefore, the correct matching is (P) $\rightarrow$ (5), (Q) $\rightarrow$ (3), (R) $\rightarrow$ (2), (S) $\rightarrow$ (4).

Answer: (P) $\rightarrow$ (5), (Q) $\rightarrow$ (3), (R) $\rightarrow$ (2), (S) $\rightarrow$ (4)

26449.text:
The binding energy of nucleons in a nucleus can be affected by the pairwise Coulomb repulsion. Assume that all nucleons are uniformly distributed inside the nucleus. Let the binding energy of a proton be ${E}_{b}^{p}$ and the binding energy of a neutron be ${E}_{b}^{n}$ in the nucleus.
Which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct?
options: ${E}_{b}^{p} - {E}_{b}^{n}$ is proportional to $Z\left(Z - 1\right)$ where $Z$ is the atomic number of the nucleus.
${E}_{b}^{p} - {E}_{b}^{n}$ is proportional to ${A}^{- \dfrac{1}{3}}$ where $A$ is the mass number of the nucleus.
${E}_{b}^{p}$ increases if the nucleus undergoes a beta decay emitting a positron.
26449.sol:
Total binding energy (without considering repulsions),

${E}_{b} = \left[Z{m}_{p} + \left(A - Z\right){m}_{n} - {m}_{x}\right]{c}^{2}$

Where, $X ZA$ is the nuclei under consideration.

Now, considering repulsion :

Number of proton pairs $= C2 Z$

$⇒$ Thus repulsion energy $∝ \dfrac{Z\left(Z - 1\right)}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{4\pi{ϵ}_{0}}\dfrac{{e}^{2}}{R}$

Where $R$ is the radius of the nucleus

$⇒ {E}_{b}^{p} - {E}_{b}^{n} ∝ Z\left(Z - 1\right) ∴$ there will be no repulsion term for neutrons.

Also, since $R = {R}_{0}A\dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ {E}_{b}^{p} - {E}_{b}^{n} ∝ {A}^{- \dfrac{1}{3}}$

Because of repulsion among protons,

${E}_{b}^{p} < {E}_{b}^{n}$

Since in ${\beta}^{+}$ decay, number of protons decrease $⇒$ repulsion would decrease

$⇒ {E}_{b}^{p}$ increases

27198.subject: Chemistry
27198.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The dipole moment of R-CN is greater than R-NC and R-NC can undergo hydrolysis under acidic medium to produce
.
Statement II: R-CN hydrolyses under acidic medium to produce a compound which on treatment with $\mathrm{SOCl}_{2}$, followed by the addition of $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ gives another compound $(\mathrm{x})$. This compound $(\mathrm{x})$ on treatment with $\mathrm{NaOCl} / \mathrm{NaOH}$ gives a product, that on treatment with $\mathrm{CHCl}_{3} / \mathrm{KOH} / \Delta$ produces R-NC.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
27198.sol:
Statement I: The dipole moment of alkyl cyanides ($R-CN$) is indeed greater than alkyl isocyanides ($R-NC$) because the $C \equiv N$ bond is more polar than the $N^+ \equiv C^-$ bond where formal charges oppose the electronegativity difference. However, the acidic hydrolysis of $R-NC$ produces a primary amine ($R-NH_2$) and formic acid ($HCOOH$), not a carboxylic acid ($R-COOH$). Thus, Statement I is false.
Statement II: $R-CN$ on acidic hydrolysis gives $R-COOH$. Treatment with $SOCl_2$ gives $R-COCl$. Addition of $NH_3$ gives $R-CONH_2$ (compound x). Treatment of $R-CONH_2$ with $NaOCl/NaOH$ (Hofmann Bromamide Degradation equivalent) gives $R-NH_2$. $R-NH_2$ on treatment with $CHCl_3/KOH/\Delta$ (Carbylamine reaction) produces $R-NC$. Thus, Statement II is true.
Therefore, Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

28370.subject: Chemistry
28370.text: Which of the following artificial sweeteners has the highest sweetness value in comparison to cane sugar?
28370.sol:
Saccharin, also called ortho-sulphobenzimide, is the first popular artificial sweetening agent. It is about 550 times as sweet as cane sugar. Its use is of great value to diabetic persons and people who need to control their intake of calories.

Aspartame is the most successful and widely used artificial sweetener. It is roughly 100 times as sweet as cane sugar. It is the methyl ester of dipeptide formed from aspartic acid and phenylalanine. Use of aspartame is limited to cold foods and soft drinks because it is unstable at cooking temperature.

Alitame is a high-potency sweetener, and it is roughly 2000 times as sweet as cane sugar.

Sucralose is trichloro derivative of sucrose. Its appearance and taste are like sugar. It is roughly 600 times as sweet as cane sugar.

So, sweetness value order with respect to cane sugar is:

Alitame > Sucralose > Saccharin > Aspartame

29534.sol: The concentration of dissolved oxygen in water is very important for aquatic life. If the concentration of dissolved oxygen of water is below 6 ppm, the growth of fish gets inhibited. The amount of oxygen required by bacteria to break down the organic matter present in a certain volume of a sample of water, is called Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD). The amount of BOD in the water is a measure of the amount of organic material in the water, in terms of how much oxygen will be required to break it down biologically. Clean water would have BOD value of less than 5 ppm whereas highly polluted water could have a BOD value of 17 ppm or more.

30400.text:
Compound (X) [styrene] is subjected to the sequence of reactions as shown above: (i) $Br_2/CHCl_3$ (ii) $NaNH_2$ excess (iii) $CH_3I$ (iv) $H_2$, $Na/NH_3$ $(l)$, giving Major Product (Y). Molar mass of the major product (Y) formed is ______ g mol$^{-1}$.
(Given molar mass in g mol$^{-1}$ C:$12$, H: $1$, O: $16$)
30400.sol:
Addition of $Br_2$ to styrene (X) yields 1,2-dibromoethylbenzene.

$C_6H_5-CH=CH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/CHCl_3} C_6H_5-CH(Br)-CH_2(Br)$

Reaction with excess $NaNH_2$ causes double dehydrohalogenation followed by deprotonation of the terminal alkyne, forming sodium phenylacetylide.

$C_6H_5-CH(Br)-CH_2(Br) \xrightarrow{NaNH_2 \text{ (excess)}} C_6H_5-C \equiv C^- Na^+$

Nucleophilic substitution with $CH_3I$ yields 1-phenylpropyne.

$C_6H_5-C \equiv C^- Na^+ \xrightarrow{CH_3I} C_6H_5-C \equiv C-CH_3$

Reduction with $Na/NH_3(l)$ reduces the internal alkyne to a trans-alkene without affecting the benzene ring.

$C_6H_5-C \equiv C-CH_3 \xrightarrow{Na/NH_3(l)} C_6H_5-CH=CH-CH_3$

The major product (Y) is trans-1-phenylpropene, which has the molecular formula $C_9H_{10}$.

Molar mass of $C_9H_{10} = (9 \times 12) + (10 \times 1) = 108 + 10 = 118 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $118$

31450.text: Portland cement contains '$X$' to enhance the setting time. What is '$X$'?
31450.sol:
Cement is an important building material. It was first introduced in England in 1824 by Joseph Aspdin. It is also called Portland cement because it resembles with the natural limestone quarried in the Isle of Portland, England.

The raw materials for the manufacture of cement are limestone and clay.

When mixed with water, the setting of cement takes place to give a hard mass. This is due to the hydration of the molecules of the constituents and their rearrangement. The purpose of adding gypsum is only to slow down the process of setting of the cement so that it gets sufficiently hardened.

Hence,Gypsum$\left({CaSO}_{4} \cdot 2{H}_{2}O\right)$ is used to enhance setting time in portland cement.

33014.text: Let $f\left(x\right)$ be a polynomial of degree four and having its extreme values at $x = 1$ and $x = 2$. If $\lim_{x \to 0}\left[1 + \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{{x}^{2}}\right] = 3$, then $f\left(2\right)$ is equal to
33014.sol:
Let $f\left(x\right) = a{x}^{4} + b{x}^{3} + c{x}^{2} + dx + e$

Then $\lim_{x \to 0}\left[1 + \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{{x}^{2}}\right] = 3$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to 0}\left[1 + a{x}^{2} + bx + c + \dfrac{d}{x} + \dfrac{e}{{x}^{2}}\right] = 3$

This limit exists when $d = e = 0$.

So, $\lim_{x \to 0}\left[1 + a{x}^{2} + bx + c\right] = 3$

$⇒ c + 1 = 3$

$⇒ c = 2$

It is given, $x = 1$ and $x = 2$ are the solution of ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 0$.

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 4a{x}^{3} + 3b{x}^{2} + 2cx$

$⇒ x\left(4a{x}^{2} + 3bx + 2c\right) = 0$

Given $1, 2$ are the roots of the quadratic equation.

$⇒ \text{Sum of roots} = \dfrac{- 3b}{4a} = 1 + 2 = 3$

$⇒ b = - 4a$

Product of roots $= \dfrac{2c}{4a} = 1 \cdot 2 = 2$

$⇒ a = \dfrac{c}{4}$

$⇒ a = \dfrac{1}{2}\text{,}b = - 2$

$∴ f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}{x}^{4} - 2{x}^{3} + 2{x}^{2}$

$⇒ f\left(2\right) = 8 - 16 + 8$

$⇒ f\left(2\right) = 0$

Equation of $RS$

34785.text: Let $y = y ( x )$ be the solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 + x{e}^{y - x}, - \sqrt{2} < x < \sqrt{2}, y\left(0\right) = 0$, then the minimum value of $y\left(x\right), x \in \left(- \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2}\right)$ is equal to :
34785.sol:
Given,

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 + x{e}^{y - x}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy - dx}{{e}^{y - x}} = xdx$

$⇒ ∫ \dfrac{d\left(y - x\right)}{{e}^{y - x}} = ∫ xdx$

$⇒ - {e}^{x - y} = \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2} + c$

At $x = 0, y = 0 ⇒ c = - 1$

So, the particular solution is

${e}^{x - y} = \dfrac{2 - {x}^{2}}{2}$

$⇒ y = x - ln\left(\dfrac{2 - {x}^{2}}{2}\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 + \dfrac{2x}{2 - {x}^{2}} = \dfrac{2 + 2x - {x}^{2}}{2 - {x}^{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{{x}^{2} - 2x - 2}{{x}^{2} - 2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{{x}^{2} - 2x - 2}{\left(x + \sqrt{2}\right)\left(x - \sqrt{2}\right)}$

If $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0 ⇒ {x}^{2} - 2x - 2 = 0$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{12}}{2}$

$⇒ x = 1 \pm \sqrt{3}$

So minimum value occurs at $x = 1 - \sqrt{3}$

$y\left(1 - \sqrt{3}\right) = \left(1 - \sqrt{3}\right) - ln\left(\dfrac{2 - ( 4 - 2\sqrt{3} )}{2}\right)$

$= \left(1 - \sqrt{3}\right) - ln\left(\sqrt{3} - 1\right)$

36955.text: If one real root of the quadratic equation $81 x^{2}+k x+256=0$ is cube of the other root, then a value of $\mathrm{k}$ is :
36955.sol:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of the equation, $81 x^{2}+k x+256=0$

Given $(\alpha)^{\frac{1}{3}}=\beta \Rightarrow \alpha=\beta^{3}$

$\because \quad$ Product of the roots $=\frac{256}{81}$

$\therefore \quad(\alpha)(\beta)=\frac{256}{81}$

$\Rightarrow \quad \beta^{4}=\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^{4} \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{4}{3} \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{64}{27}$

$\because$ Sum of the roots $=-\frac{k}{81}$

$\therefore \quad \alpha+\beta=-\frac{k}{81} \Rightarrow \frac{4}{3}+\frac{64}{27}=-\frac{k}{81}$

$\Rightarrow \quad k=-300$

A. $l=30 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~b}=1 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~d}=1 \mu \mathrm{~m}$
B. $l=3 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~b}=1 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~d}=30 \mu \mathrm{~m}$
C. $l=6 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~b}=5 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~d}=3 \mu \mathrm{~m}$
D. $l=1 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~b}=1 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~d}=10 \mu \mathrm{~m}$
E. $l=5 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~b}=2 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~d}=1 \mu \mathrm{~m}$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
39115.sol: We know $C=\frac{A \varepsilon_0}{d}$ $=\frac{b \ell \varepsilon_0}{d}$ So to increase the capacitance by 10 factor $\left(\frac{A}{d}\right)$ has to increase by 10 fator. For option (A) $\quad C^{\prime}=\frac{(30 \ell) b \varepsilon_0}{\left(\frac{d}{3}\right)}=30 \mathrm{C}$ For option (B) $\quad C^{\prime}=\frac{\ell b \varepsilon_0}{10 d}=\frac{C}{10}$ For option (C) $\quad C^{\prime}=\frac{(2 \ell) 5 b \varepsilon_0}{d}=10 \mathrm{C}$ For option (D) $\quad C^{\prime}=\frac{\left(\frac{\ell}{3}\right) b \varepsilon_0}{\left(\frac{10 d}{3}\right)}=\frac{C}{10}$ For option (E) $\quad C^{\prime}=\frac{\left(\frac{\ell}{3}\right) 5(2 b) \varepsilon_0}{\left(\frac{d}{3}\right)}=10 C$ Clearly (C) and (E) are the situation for 10 C

39672.text: Eight copper wire of length $l$ and diameter d are joined in parallel to form a single composite conductor of resistance $R$. If a single copper wire of length $2l$ have the same resistance $\left(R\right)$ then its diameter will be _____ $d$.
39672.sol:
Each wire has resistance, $r = ρ\dfrac{4l}{\pi{d}^{2}}$

Eight wire in parallel, then equivalent resistance is

$R = \dfrac{r}{8} = \dfrac{ρl}{2\pi{d}^{2}}$

Single copper wire of length $2l$ has resistance $R = ρ\dfrac{2l \times 4}{\pi{d}_{1}^{2}}$.

Comparing both equations, we get,

$ρ\dfrac{8l}{\pi{d}_{1}^{2}} = \dfrac{ρl}{2\pi{d}^{2}}$

$⇒ {d}_{1} = 4d$

40434.subject: Physics
40434.text: A three coulomb charge moves from the point $(0, -2, -5)$ to the point $(5, 1, 2)$ in an electric field expressed as $\vec{E} = 2x\hat{i} + 3y^2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ N/C. The work done in moving the charge is _______ J.
40434.sol:
The force experienced by the charge in the electric field is given by $\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$.

Given $q = 3$ C and $\vec{E} = 2x\hat{i} + 3y^2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ N/C, the force is:
$\vec{F} = 3(2x\hat{i} + 3y^2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}) = 6x\hat{i} + 9y^2\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}$ N

The work done by the electric field in moving the charge is:
$W = \int \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F_x dx + \int_{y_1}^{y_2} F_y dy + \int_{z_1}^{z_2} F_z dz$

Substituting the limits from the initial point $(0, -2, -5)$ to the final point $(5, 1, 2)$:
$W = \int_{0}^{5} 6x dx + \int_{-2}^{1} 9y^2 dy + \int_{-5}^{2} 12 dz$

Evaluating each integral separately:
$\int_{0}^{5} 6x dx = \left[ 3x^2 \right]_{0}^{5} = 3(5^2 - 0^2) = 75$ J

$\int_{-2}^{1} 9y^2 dy = \left[ 3y^3 \right]_{-2}^{1} = 3(1^3 - (-2)^3) = 3(1 - (-8)) = 3(9) = 27$ J

$\int_{-5}^{2} 12 dz = \left[ 12z \right]_{-5}^{2} = 12(2 - (-5)) = 12(7) = 84$ J

Total work done $W = 75 + 27 + 84 = 186$ J.

Answer: $186$

41632.subject: Physics
41632.text: Two coaxial solenoids of different radii carry current $I$ in the same direction. Let $\overset{\to}{{F}_{1}}$ be the magnetic force on the inner solenoid due to the outer one and $\overset{\to}{{F}_{2}}$ be the magnetic force on the outer solenoid due to the inner one. Then:
options: $\overset{\to}{{F}_{1}}$  is radially inwards and  $\overset{\to}{{F}_{2}}$  is radially outwards
41632.sol:
${S}_{2}$ is a solenoid with more radius than ${S}_{1}$, the magnetic field of the solenoid ${S}_{2}$ will be along the axis and constant, so the magnetic force on an element of solenoid ${S}_{1}$ will be,

$d \overset{\to}{F}1 = i\left(\overset{\to}{l} \times \overset{\to}{B}\right)$

$d \overset{\to}{F}1 = ilB\left(\overset{^}{j} \times \left(- \overset{^}{i}\right)\right) = iBl\overset{^}{k}$

Similarly, for just next coil the magnetic field is in same direction, but the current element is in opposite direction, so,

$d \overset{\to}{F}1 = ilB\left(- \overset{^}{j} \times \left(- \overset{^}{i}\right)\right) = - iBl\overset{^}{k}$.

From Symmetry, we can say that the overall force will be cancelled to the whole coil, hence, $\overset{\to}{F}1 = 0$

Similarly, from coil ${S}_{1}$ to ${S}_{2}$, The magnetic field of the inner solenoid is symmetric about its axis, but not exactly along the axis of the outer solenoid. As the outer solenoid is placed symmetrically the push of any coil will be equal and opposite to the pull of coil placed exactly the opposite distance from the centre. Hence, the net force on the outer coil will be zero, i.e., $\overset{\to}{F}2 = 0$.

${A}_{A}{V}_{A} = {A}_{B}{V}_{B}$

So, $1 . 5 \times {10}^{- 4} \times {V}_{A} = 25 \times {10}^{- 6} \times {V}_{B}$

${V}_{A} = \dfrac{25 \times {10}^{- 6}}{1 . 5 \times {10}^{- 4}} \times 0 . 6$

$= \dfrac{1}{10}m{s}^{- 1}$

Substituting in equation (i)

$⇒ {P}_{A} - {P}_{B} = \dfrac{1000}{2}\left[0 . {6}^{2} - 0 . {1}^{2}\right] = \dfrac{1000}{2} \times 0 . 7 \times 0 . 5$

$= 175Pa$

42185.subject: Physics
42185.text: A gas balloon is going up with a constant velocity of $10$ m/s. When this balloon reached a height of $75$ m, a stone is dropped from it and balloon keeps moving up with the same velocity. The height of the balloon when the stone hits the ground is ________ m. (Take $g=10$ m/s$^2$)
42185.sol:
When the stone is dropped, it acquires the initial velocity of the balloon. Taking the upward direction as positive, the initial velocity of the stone is $u = 10$ m/s.

The displacement of the stone when it hits the ground is $S = -75$ m, and its acceleration is $a = -g = -10$ m/s$^2$.

Using the equation of motion $S = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$:

$-75 = 10t - \dfrac{1}{2}(10)t^2$

$-75 = 10t - 5t^2$

$5t^2 - 10t - 75 = 0$

$t^2 - 2t - 15 = 0$

$(t - 5)(t + 3) = 0$

Since time cannot be negative, $t = 5$ s.

During this time, the balloon continues to move upwards with a constant velocity of $10$ m/s. The distance travelled by the balloon in $5$ s is:

$d = v \times t = 10 \times 5 = 50$ m

The total height of the balloon when the stone hits the ground is:

$H = 75 + 50 = 125$ m

Answer: $125$

42762.text: The point $A$ moves with a uniform speed along the circumference of a circle of radius $0 . 36m$ and covers $30 °$ in $0 . 1s$. The perpendicular projection $P$ from $A$ on the diameter $MN$ represents the simple harmonic motion of $P$. The restoration force per unit mass when $P$ touches $M$ will be :
42762.sol:
The point $A$ covers $30 ° in 0 . 1s$.
Then, we have $\dfrac{\pi}{6}rad ⟶ 0 . 1s$.
Or $1rad ⟶ \dfrac{0 . 1}{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}s$
Or $2\piin \to \dfrac{0 . 1 \times 6}{\pi} \times 2\pi$
Thus, time taken is $T = 1 . 2sec .

We know that $\omega = $\dfrac{2\pi}{T}
Then, $\omega = $\dfrac{2\pi}{1 . 2}
Restoration force $( F ) = {m \omega}^{2}A .

Then Restoration force per unit mass $\left(\dfrac{F}{m}\right) = {\omega}^{2}A$
$\left(\dfrac{F}{m}\right) = {\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{1 . 2}\right)}^{2} \times 0 . 36$

$≅ 9 . 87N$

44053.text:
Consider a modified Bernoulli equation.
$\left(\mathrm{P}+\frac{A}{B t^{2}}\right)+\rho g(h+B t)+\frac{1}{2} \rho V^{2}=$ constant

44053.sol:
All terms must have dimension of pressure $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$.
For $(h + Bt)$: Since $\rho gh$ has dimension of pressure, $[h] = [L]$.
For dimensional consistency: $[Bt] = [L]$, so $[B] = [LT^{-1}] = [M^0LT^{-1}]$
For $\frac{A}{Bt^2}$: $\frac{[A]}{[B][T^2]} = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$
$[A] = [B][T^2][ML^{-1}T^{-2}] = [LT^{-1}][T^2][ML^{-1}T^{-2}] = [ML^0T^{-1}]$
$[A] = [ML^0T^{-1}]$ and $[B] = [M^0LT^{-1}]$

46222.text: If the electric flux entering and leaving an enclosed surface respectively are $\phi$, and $\phi_2$, the electric charge inside the surface will be
46222.sol:
According to Gauss theorem "the net electric flux through any closed surface is equal to the net charge inside the surface divided by $\varepsilon_0{ }^{\prime \prime}$.
Therefore, $\quad \phi \propto \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$
Let $-q_1$ be the charge, due to which flux $\phi_1$ is entering the surface,
$\phi_1=\frac{-q_1}{\varepsilon_0} -q_1=\varepsilon_0 \phi_1$
Let $+q_2$ be the charge, due to which flux $\phi_2$ is entering the surface.
$\phi_2=\frac{q_2}{\varepsilon_0}
or \quad q_2=\varepsilon_0 \phi_2$
So, electric charge inside the surface
$=q_2-q_1 \begin{aligned} & =\varepsilon_0 \phi_2+\varepsilon_0 \phi_1 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad=\varepsilon_0\left(\phi_2+\phi_1\right) \end{aligned}$

46575.subject: Physics
46575.text: A ball of radius $R$ rolls without slipping. Find the fraction of total energy associated with its rotational energy, if the radius of the gyration of the ball about an axis passing through its centre of mass is $K$.
46575.sol:
Kinetic energy of rotation is
$K_{\text{rot }}=\frac{1}{2} l \omega^2=\frac{1}{2} M K^2 \frac{v^2}{R^2}$
where, $k$ is radius of gyration.
Kinetic energy of translation is $K_{\text{trans }}=\frac{1}{2} M v^2$
Thus total energy,
$\begin{aligned} E & =K_{\text{rot }}+K_{\text{trans }} \\ & =\frac{1}{2} M K^2 \frac{v^2}{R^2}+\frac{1}{2} M v^2 \\ & =\frac{1}{2} M v^2\left(\frac{K^2}{R^2}+1\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \frac{M v^2}{R^2}\left(K^2+R^2\right)\end{aligned}$
Hence, $\begin{aligned} \frac{K_{\text{rot }}}{\text{ Total energy, } E} & =\frac{\frac{1}{2} M K^2 \frac{v^2}{R^2}}{\frac{1}{2} \frac{M v^2}{R^2}\left(K^2+R^2\right)} \\ & =\frac{K^2}{K^2+R^2}\end{aligned}$

$p_{i A}=\frac{p_{i B}}{1.5}=\frac{2}{3} p_{i B}\Rightarrow \quad m_A=\frac{2}{3} m B\Rightarrow \quad 3 m_A=2 m B \quad[\because p \propto m]$

56007.subject: Chemistry
56007.text: Identify a type of order of reaction that its unit of rate constant is mol dm^{-3}$ s^{-1}$ from the following.
56007.sol:
The general formula for the unit of the rate constant $k$ for an $n$-th order reaction is given by $(\text{concentration})^{1-n} \text{time}^{-1}$.

Using the standard units of concentration as $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and time as $\text{s}$, the unit of $k$ becomes $(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{1-n} \texts^{-1}$.

The given unit of the rate constant is $\text{mol dm}^{-3}\texts^{-1}$.

Comparing the powers of the concentration term, we get:

$1 - n = 1$

$n = 0$

Therefore, the reaction is a zero-order reaction.

Answer: Zero-order reaction

61314.text: The differential equation representing the family of parabolas having vertex at the origin and axis along the positive Y-axis is
61314.sol:
Family of parabolas with vertex at origin and axis along positive Y-axis: $x^2 = 4ay$ where $a$ is an arbitrary constant.

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ yields:

$2x = 4a \frac{dy}{dx}$

Eliminate $a$ by substituting $4a = \frac{x^2}{y}$ (for $y \neq 0$):

$2x = \left(\frac{x^2}{y}\right) \frac{dy}{dx}$

Multiplying both sides by $y$ and dividing by $x$ (for $x \neq 0$):

$2y = x \frac{dy}{dx}$

Rewriting gives the differential equation:

$x \frac{dy}{dx} - 2y = 0$

This corresponds to option A.

The differential equation is given as $(1 + y^2) + (x - e^{\tan^{-1} y}) \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$. Rearranging to express in terms of $\frac{dx}{dy}$ yields:

This is linear in $x$ with $P(y) = \frac{1}{1 + y^2}$ and $Q(y) = \frac{e^{\tan^{-1} y}}{1 + y^2}$. The integrating factor is $e^{\int P(y) \, dy} = e^{\tan^{-1} y}$, leading to the solution:

$x \cdot e^{\tan^{-1} y} = \int e^{2\tan^{-1} y} \cdot \frac{dy}{1 + y^2} + C$.

Let $u = \tan^{-1} y$, so $du = \frac{dy}{1 + y^2}$, simplifying the integral to $\int e^{2u} \, du = \frac{1}{2} e^{2u} = \frac{1}{2} e^{2\tan^{-1} y}$. Thus:

$x e^{\tan^{-1} y} = \frac{1}{2} e^{2\tan^{-1} y} + C$.

Multiplying by 2 and letting $k = 2C$, we have $2x e^{\tan^{-1} y} = e^{2\tan^{-1} y} + k$, which corresponds to option A.

61806.text: For $x > 1$, if $(2 x)^{2 y}=4 \mathrme^{2 x-2 y}$, then $(1+\log 2 x)^2 \frac{d y}{d x}$ is equal to
61806.sol:
$(2 x)^{2 y}=4 \mathrme^{2 x-2 y}$
Taking log on both sides, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& 2 y \log 2 x=\log \left(4 \mathrme^{2 x-2 y}\right) \\
& \Rightarrow 2 y \log 2 x=\log 4+\log \mathrme^{2 x-2 y} \\
& \Rightarrow 2 y \log 2 x=\log 4+2 x-2 y \\
& \Rightarrow 2 y \log 2 x+2 y=\log 4+2 x \\
& \Rightarrow 2(y \log 2 x+y)=2 \log 2+2 x \\
& \Rightarrow y \log 2 x+y=\log 2+x \\
& \Rightarrow y(1+\log 2 x)=x+\log 2 \\
& \Rightarrow y=\frac{x+\log 2}{1+\log 2 x}
\end{aligned}$
Differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=\frac{(1+\log 2 x)(1+0)-(x+\log 2)\left(\frac{1}{2 x}\right) \cdot 2}{(1+\log 2 x)^2} \\
\Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=\frac{(1+\log 2 x)-\frac{1}{x}(x+\log 2)}{(1+\log 2 x)^2} \\
\Rightarrow(1+\log 2 x)^2 \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=1+\log 2 x-1-\frac{\log 2}{x} \\
\Rightarrow(1+\log 2 x)^2 \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=\log 2 x-\frac{\log 2}{x} \\
=\frac{x \log 2 x-\log 2}{x}
\end{gathered}$

options: $\frac{1}{2} \tan ^{-1}(\tan x)+c \quad, \quad$ where $c$ is the constant of integration.

$\frac{1}{4} \tan ^{-1}(\tan x)+\mathrm{c}, \quad$ where c is the constant of integration.
62217.sol:
Let $I = \int \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{3 \cos 2x + 5}$. Using the trigonometric substitution $\cos 2x = \frac{1 - \tan^2 x}{1 + \tan^2 x}$, we transform the integral:

$I = \int \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{3\left(\frac{1 - \tan^2 x}{1 + \tan^2 x}\right) + 5} = \int \frac{1 + \tan^2 x}{8 + 2\tan^2 x}\mathrm{d}x$.

Recognizing that $1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x$, we have $I = \int \frac{\sec^2 x \mathrm{d}x}{8 + 2\tan^2 x}$. With the substitution $t = \tan x$, where $\mathrm{d}t = \sec^2 x \mathrm{d}x$, the integral becomes:

$I = \int \frac{\mathrm{d}t}{8 + 2t^2} = \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{\mathrm{d}t}{4 + t^2}$.

Applying the standard antiderivative formula $\int \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{a^2 + u^2} = \frac{1}{a} \arctan \left(\frac{u}{a}\right) + C$ with $a = 2$, we obtain:

$I = \frac{1}{4} \arctan \left(\frac{t}{2}\right) + C$.

Substituting back $t = \tan x$ gives:

$I = \frac{1}{4} \arctan \left(\frac{\tan x}{2}\right) + C$.

This result corresponds to option C.

62920.text: If $\sim p \to q$ is false and $q \leftrightarrow r$ is false, then the truth value of $(p, q, r)$ is...
62920.sol:
The implication $\sim p \to q$ is given as false.

An implication $A \to B$ is false if and only if $A$ is true and $B$ is false.

Therefore, $\sim p$ is true and $q$ is false.

Since $\sim p$ is true, $p$ must be false (F$). Thus, $p = F$ and $q = F$.

The biconditional $q \leftrightarrow r$ is given as false.

A biconditional $A \leftrightarrow B$ is false if and only if $A$ and $B$ have opposite truth values.

Since $q$ is false, $r$ must be true (T$).

The truth values of $(p, q, r)$ are $(F, F, T)$.

Answer: $(F, F, T)$

62930.text: The contrapositive of the statement pattern $[p \vee (p \to q)] \to (p \wedge \sim q)$ is
62930.sol:
Let the given statement be $X \to Y$, where $X = p \vee (p \to q)$ and $Y = p \wedge \sim q$.

The contrapositive of $X \to Y$ is $\sim Y \to \sim X$.

First, we find $\sim Y$:
$\sim Y = \sim (p \wedge \sim q) = \sim p \vee q$

Next, we find $\sim X$:
$\sim X = \sim [p \vee (p \to q)]$
Using De Morgan's Law, we get:
$\sim X = \sim p \wedge \sim (p \to q)$

Since $p \to q \equiv \sim p \vee q$, its negation is $\sim (p \to q) \equiv p \wedge \sim q$.
Substituting this back, we get:
$\sim X = \sim p \wedge (p \wedge \sim q)$

Therefore, the contrapositive $\sim Y \to \sim X$ is:
$(\sim p \vee q) \to [\sim p \wedge (p \wedge \sim q)]$

63640.subject: Mathematics
63640.text: A coin is tossed until one head appears or a tail appears 4 times in succession. The probability distribution of the number of tosses is
63640.sol:
The process terminates when a head appears or four consecutive tails occur. The number of tosses, $X$, has possible values $1$, $2$, $3$, and $4$.

An outcome of a head on the first toss gives $X = 1$, with probability $P(X=1) = \frac{1}{2}$.

For $X = 2$, the sequence is $TH$, so $P(X=2) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}$.

For $X = 3$, the sequence is $TTH$, giving $P(X=3) = (\frac{1}{2})^3 = \frac{1}{8}$.

$X = 4$ occurs either with $TTTH$ or $TTTT$, each with probability $(\frac{1}{2})^4 = \frac{1}{16}$, so $P(X=4) = \frac{1}{16} + \frac{1}{16} = \frac{1}{8}$.

Summing the probabilities confirms $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = 1$.

The probability distribution matches Option D.

64386.text: If the lines $\vec{r} = (\hat{i} + m\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}) + \lambda(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r} = (4\hat{i} + \hat{j}) + \mu(5\hat{i} + m\hat{j} + \hat{k})$ intersect each other, then m =
64386.sol:
Equating the position vectors of the two lines for intersection:

$1 + 2\lambda = 4 + 5\mu$

$m + 3\lambda = 1 + m\mu$

$3 + 4\lambda = \mu$

From the third equation, $\mu = 4\lambda + 3$.

Substituting this into the first equation:

$2\lambda - 5(4\lambda + 3) = 3$

$-18\lambda - 15 = 3$

$-18\lambda = 18 \Rightarrow \lambda = -1$

Substituting $\lambda = -1$ into $\mu = 4\lambda + 3$ gives $\mu = -1$.

Now, substituting $\lambda = -1$ and $\mu = -1$ into the second equation:

$m + 3(-1) = 1 + m(-1)$

$m - 3 = 1 - m$

$2m = 4 \Rightarrow m = 2$

Answer: $2$

65611.text:
An alternating e.m.f. is given by $e=e_0 \sin \omega t$. In how much time the e.m.f. will have half its maximum value, if e starts from zero ?

The alternating e.m.f. is characterized by $e = e_0 \sin \omega t$.

For $e = \frac{e_0}{2}$, solving $\sin \omega t = \frac{1}{2}$ yields $\omega t = \frac{\pi}{6}$.

Substituting $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ gives $\frac{2\pi}{T} t = \frac{\pi}{6}$, from which $t = \frac{T}{12}$.

The e.m.f. reaches half its maximum at $t = \frac{T}{12}$ from zero.

66209.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
66209.text: Three rods of same mass are placed as shown in figure. The co-ordinates of centre of mass of the system are
66209.sol:
The center of mass coordinates for the system of three uniform rods, each of mass $M$, are determined by locating each rod's center and applying the weighted average formula.

The vertical rod from $(0,0) to (0,a)$ has center at $\left(0, \frac{a}{2}\right)$.

The horizontal rod from $(0,0) to (2a,0)$ has center at $(a, 0)$.

The hypotenuse rod from $(0,a) to (2a,0)$ has center at $\left(a, \frac{a}{2}\right)$.

With total mass $3M$, the system's center of mass coordinates are:

$X_{CM} = \frac{M(0) + M(a) + M(a)}{3M} = \frac{2a}{3}$

$Y_{CM} = \frac{M \left(\frac{a}{2}\right) +$M(0) + M $\left(\frac{a}{2}\right)}{3M} = \frac{a}{3}$

The result $\left(\frac{2a}{3}, \frac{a}{3}\right)$corresponds to option D.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{D}}$

69195.subject: Physics
69195.text: A thin metal wire of length ' $L$ ' and mass ' $M$ ' is bent to form semicircular ring as shown. The moment of inertia about $\mathrm{XX}^1$ is
69195.sol:
The moment of inertia about a diameter of a semicircular ring of mass $M$ and length $L$ requires relating the geometric parameters. For a semicircle of radius $R$, the arc length gives $L = \pi R$, so $R = L / \pi$.

The moment of inertia about diameter $XX'$ is derived by integration. A mass element $dm = (M / \pi) d\theta$ at angle $\theta$ has perpendicular distance $R \sin \theta$ from the axis, contributing $dI = dm \cdot (R \sin \theta)^2 = (M R^2 / \pi) \sin^2 \theta d\theta$.

Integrating from $0$ to $\pi$:

$I = \frac{M R^2}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \sin^2 \theta d\theta = \frac{M R^2}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \frac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2} d\theta = \frac{M R^2}{2\pi} \left[ \theta - \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2} \right]_0^\pi = \frac{M R^2}{2}$

Substituting $R = L / \pi$ yields:

$I = \frac{M}{2} \left( \frac{L}{\pi} \right)^2 = \frac{M L^2}{2\pi^2}$

Final answer: $\frac{M L^2}{2\pi^2}$

70507.text: A pipe open at both ends of length 1.5 m is dipped in water at one end such that $2^{\text{nd }}$ overtone of vibrating air column is resonating with a tuning fork of frequency 330 Hz. The length of the pipe immersed in water is (Speed of sound in air $=330 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}  ) (Neglect end correction)$
70507.sol:
A pipe open at both ends and partly immersed in water functions as a closed organ pipe.

The resonant frequencies of a closed pipe are $f_n = \frac{(2n-1)v}{4l}$, where $n$ is the harmonic number, $v$ is the speed of sound, and $l$ is the length of the air column.

The second overtone corresponds to the third harmonic ($n=3$).

Given $f = 330\,\text{Hz}$ and $v = 330\,\text{m/s}$, for resonance with the second overtone:

$330 = \frac{5 \times 330}{4l}$

Simplifying, $1 = \frac{5}{4l}$, so $l = \frac{5}{4} = 1.25\,\text{m}$.

The total pipe length is $1.5\,\text{m}$, so the immersed length is $1.5 - 1.25 = 0.25\,\text{m}$.

This corresponds to option D.

71028.subject: Biology
71028.text: Cleavage differs from normal mitotic divisions as
options: There is no nuclear division during cleavage.
There is no division of cytoplasm during cleavage.
There is no growth phase between the cleavages.
The division of cytoplasm follows nuclear division.
71028.sol:
Cleavage is a series of rapid mitotic divisions of the zygote characterized by the absence of growth phases (G1 and G2 phases) between successive divisions.

Due to the lack of a growth phase, the total volume or size of the embryo remains constant, while the number of cells increases and the size of individual cells (blastomeres) decreases.

In normal mitotic divisions, a distinct growth phase occurs where the cell grows to its original size before undergoing the next division.

Answer: There is no growth phase between the cleavages.

71265.subject: Biology
71265.text: What is the role of the DHU arm of a tRNA molecule?
71265.sol:
The tRNA molecule has several specific regions with distinct functions:

The DHU loop (dihydrouridine loop) acts as the recognition site for the specific aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase enzyme, which is responsible for adding the correct amino acid. Hence, it is known as the amino acid recognition site.

The 3' end (CCA sequence) is the amino acid binding site where the amino acid physically attaches.

The anticodon loop is the codon recognition site that pairs with the mRNA codon.

The T$\Psi$ C loop is the ribosome recognition site.

Answer: Amino acid recognition site.

71473.text: Formation of the megaspore from the megaspore mother cell involves a __________.
71473.sol:
The process of formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell (MMC) is called megasporogenesis.

The megaspore mother cell is a diploid cell (2n$) that undergoes meiotic division (meiosis) to form a linear tetrad of four haploid megaspores (n$).

Therefore, the formation of the megaspore from the megaspore mother cell involves meiosis only.

Answer: meiosis only

72036.subject: Chemistry
72036.text: What would be the heat released in kJ when $450\ \text{cm}^3$ of $0.02\ \text{M}\ \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is mixed with $650\ \text{cm}^3$ of $0.1\text{M}\ \text{NaOH}$? (Heat of neutralization of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{NaOH}$ is $-114\ \text{kJ/mol}$ of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$)
72036.sol:
Number of moles of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 = M \times V = 0.02 \times 0.450 = 0.009\ \text{mol}$

Number of moles of $\text{NaOH} = M \times V = 0.1 \times 0.650 = 0.065\ \text{mol}$

The neutralization reaction is:

$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$

From the stoichiometry, $0.009\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ requires $0.018\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{NaOH}$. Since $0.065\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{NaOH}$ is available, $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is the limiting reagent.

Heat released per mole of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is $114\ \text{kJ}$.

Total heat released $= 0.009 \times 114 = 1.026\ \text{kJ}$

Answer: $1.026$

Substituting the values:

$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + \left(R - \dfrac{R}{2}\right)^2}$

$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + \left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)^2} = \sqrt{R^2 + \dfrac{R^2}{4}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2} R$

The phase difference $\phi$ between voltage and current is given by:

$\tan \phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$

$\tan \phi = \dfrac{R - \dfrac{R}{2}}{R} = \dfrac{\dfrac{R}{2}}{R} = 0.5$

$\phi = \tan^{-1}(0.5)$

Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\ R, \tan^{-1}(0.5)$

72255.text: A closely wound solenoid of $1000$ turns and area of cross-section $2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$ carries a current of $2$ A. It is suspended through its centre and perpendicular to its length, allowing it to turn in a horizontal plane in a uniform magnetic field $5 \times 10^{-2}$ T making an angle of $60^{}^{\circ}$ with the axis of solenoid. The torque on a solenoid will be nearly $\left(\sin 60^{}^{\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$
72255.sol:
The magnetic moment of the solenoid is given by $M = NIA$

Substituting the given values:

$M = 1000 \times 2 \times 2 \times 10^{-4} = 0.4\ \text{A m}^2$

The torque acting on the solenoid in a uniform magnetic field is given by $\tau = MB \sin \theta$

Substituting the values:

$\tau = 0.4 \times 5 \times 10^{-2} \times \sin 60^{}^{\circ}$

$\tau = 2 \times 10^{-2} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$\tau = \sqrt{3} \times 10^{-2} \approx 1.732 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{Nm}$

Answer: $1.7 \times 10^{-2}$ Nm

72307.subject: Physics
72307.text: When a nucleus in an atom undergoes a radioactive decay, the atomic number and/or mass number of the atom
options: do not change for any type of radioactivity.
change for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ radiations but not for $\gamma$ radiation.
change for $\alpha$ radiation but not for others.
change for $\beta$ radiation but not for others.
72307.sol:
In $\alpha$ decay, the atomic number decreases by $2$ and the mass number decreases by $4$.

In $\beta$ decay, the atomic number changes by $1$ (increases in $\beta^{-}$ and decreases in $\beta^{+}$) while the mass number remains unchanged.

In $\gamma$ decay, neither the atomic number nor the mass number changes, as it only involves a transition between nuclear energy levels.

Thus, the atomic number and/or mass number change for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ radiations but not for $\gamma$ radiation.

Answer: change for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ radiations but not for $\gamma$ radiation.

76591.subject: Mathematics
76591.text:
Passage: Let $u$ be a positive integer and $f$ be a real number lying between $0 and 1$. Further, $\left(\sqrt{2}+1\right)^{10}=u+f$ and $\left(\sqrt{2}-1\right)^{10}=v$.

Question: What is the value of $(v+f)$ ?
76591.sol:
Given $(\sqrt{2}+1)^{10} = u+f$ and $(\sqrt{2}-1)^{10} = v$.

Adding both equations:

$u+f+v = (\sqrt{2}+1)^{10} + (\sqrt{2}-1)^{10}$

Expanding using the binomial theorem:

$u+f+v = 2 [^{10}C_0 (\sqrt{2})^{10} + ^{10}C_2 (\sqrt{2})^8 + \dots + ^{10}C_{10}]$

The right hand side is an even integer. Let it be $2k$.

$u+f+v = 2k$

$f+v = 2k - u$

Since $2k$ and $u$ are integers, $f+v$ must be an integer.

We are given $0 < f < 1$.

Also, $0 < \sqrt{2}-1 < 1 \Rightarrow 0 < (\sqrt{2}-1)^{10} < 1 \Rightarrow 0 < v < 1$.

Adding the inequalities for $f$ and $v$:

$0 < f+v < 2$

Since $f+v$ is an integer strictly between $0$ and $2$, the only possible value is $1$.

Therefore, $v+f = 1$.

Answer: $1$

80028.sol:
Molybdenum is absorbed as molybdate by plants. It is involved in nitrogen metabolism including nitrogen fixation. It is a component of enzyme nitrogenase and acts as enzyme activator. Its deficiency causes chlorosis and necrosis, whiptail of cauliflower and premature leaf fall.
Copper is absorbed by the plant in ionic form. Its deficiency causes necrosis, die back in Citrus, reclamation in legumes.
Manganese is absorbed by the plants as bivalent ion. It acts as enzyme activator. Its deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis as well as yellowing of starch and their subsequent degenerate.
Zinc is needed for biosynthsis of IAA and also acts as enzyme activator. Its deficiency causes chlorosis, little leaf,rosette, white bud of maize and mottling of leaves.

Chlorine of vinyl chloride $\left(\mathrm{CH}_2=\right. \mathrm{CHCl}$ ) is non-reactive (less reactive) towards nucleophile in nucleophilic substitution reaction because it shows resonance due to $+\mathrm{M}$ effect of $-\mathrm{Cl}$ atom.
In structure II, Cl-atom have positive charge and partial double bond character with $\mathrm{C}$ of vinyl group, so it is more tightly attracted towards the nucleus and it does not get replaced by nucleophile in $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}$ reaction. Related Theory $s p^3$-hybridized electrophile must have a leaving group $(\mathrm{X})$ in order for the reaction to take place.

82818.subject: Physics
82818.text: The mean free path of molecules in an ideal gas A is half that of another ideal gas B. The diameter of the spherical molecules of gas A is twice the diameter of the molecules of B. If number densities of the gases A and B are $n_A$ and $n_B$, respectively, then the correct option is :
82818.sol:
The mean free path of a gas molecule is given by $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$

Given $\lambda_A = \dfrac{1}{2}\lambda_B$ and $d_A = 2d_B$

Substituting the formula for mean free path:

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d_A^2 n_A} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d_B^2 n_B} \right)$

$\dfrac{1}{d_A^2 n_A} = \dfrac{1}{2 d_B^2 n_B}$

Substituting $d_A = 2d_B$:

$\dfrac{1}{(2d_B)^2 n_A} = \dfrac{1}{2 d_B^2 n_B}$

$\dfrac{1}{4 d_B^2 n_A} = \dfrac{1}{2 d_B^2 n_B}$

$4 n_A = 2 n_B$

$n_A = \dfrac{1}{2} n_B$

Answer: $n_A=\dfrac{1}{2}n_B$

83301.text: A point performs simple harmonic oscillation of period $T$ and the equation of motion is given by $x=a \sin (\omega t+ \frac{\pi}{6})$. After the elapse of what fraction of the time period the velocity of the point will be equal to half of its maximum velocity?
83301.sol:
Key Idea : Velocity is the time derivative of displacement.
Writing the given equation of a point performing SHM
$x=a \sin \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$
Differentiating Eq. (i), w.r.t. time, we obtain
$y=\frac{d x}{d t}=a \omega \cos \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$
It is given that $y=\frac{a \omega}{2}$, so that
or $\frac{a \omega}{2}=a \omega \cos \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$
$\frac{1}{2}=\cos \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$
or $\cos \frac{\pi}{3}=\cos \left(\omega t+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$
$\begin{array}{ll}
\text{or } & \omega t+\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{3} \\
\Rightarrow & \omega t=\frac{\pi}{6} \\
\text{or } & t=\frac{\pi}{6 \omega}=\frac{\pi \times T}{6 \times 2 \pi}=\frac{T}{12}
\end{array}$
Thus, at $\frac{T}{12}$ velocity of the point will be equal to half of its maximum velocity.

86856.subject: Physics
86856.text: A spherical glass bottle having negligible wall thickness is placed in air. When the bottle is completely filled with water, its focal length is $f$. If the water is replaced by another transparent liquid of higher refractive index, then the focal length changes to $f'$. Then the correct option is
86856.sol:
The spherical glass bottle with negligible wall thickness filled with liquid acts as a solid liquid sphere of radius $R$.

The system can be considered as a thick lens with two spherical refracting surfaces of radius $R$ and $-R$, separated by a distance $t = 2R$.

The power of the first surface is $P_1 = \dfrac{\mu - 1}{R}$ and the second surface is $P_2 = \dfrac{1 - \mu}{-R} = \dfrac{\mu - 1}{R}$.

The equivalent power of the spherical lens is given by:

$P = P_1 + P_2 - \dfrac{t}{\mu} P_1 P_2$

$P = \dfrac{2(\mu - 1)}{R} - \dfrac{2R}{\mu} \left( \dfrac{\mu - 1}{R} \right)^2$

$P = \dfrac{2(\mu - 1)}{R} \left( 1 - \dfrac{\mu - 1}{\mu} \right) = \dfrac{2(\mu - 1)}{\mu R}$

The focal length $f$ is the reciprocal of the equivalent power:

$f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{\mu R}{2(\mu - 1)} = \dfrac{R}{2} \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\mu - 1} \right)

When the water is replaced by a liquid of higher refractive index, $\mu$ increases. As $\mu$ increases, the term \dfrac{1}{\mu - 1} decreases, which implies that the focal length $ f$ decreases.

Therefore, $f' < f$.

Answer: $f' < f

Elastomers or rubbers have the weakest intermolecular forces of attraction followed by plastics while fibres have the strongest forces of attraction. Thus, the increasing intermolecular forces of attraction follows the order

elastomer < plastic < fibre.

89202.subject: Chemistry
89202.text: A crystalline solid is made of X, Y and Z. Atoms of X are present in ccp lattice; Y occupies all the octahedral voids and Z occupies all the tetrahedral voids. If all atoms along a body diagonal are removed then the formula of solid will be
89202.sol:
Number of X-atoms in unit cell = 4
Number of Y-atoms = 4
Number of Z atoms = 8
If atoms along one body diagonal are removed then 2 from corners X, 1 from body center Y and 2 neat two corners Z atoms will be absent.
Effective number of atoms may be calculated as
$X = 4 - 2 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{15}{4}$
$Y = 4 - 1 = 3$
$Z = 8 - 2 = 6$
Simplex ratio $= X: Y: Z$
$= \dfrac{15}{4}: 3: 6$
$= 5: 4: 8$
Simplest formula $= {X}_{5}{Y}_{4}{Z}_{8}$.

91696.sol:
$\alpha + \beta = {α}^{2} + {β}^{2} & \alpha\beta = {α}^{2}{β}^{2} ⇒ \alpha\beta = 0$ or 1.

If $\alpha\beta = 0,$ then let, $\alpha = 0 ⇒ \beta = 0$ or 1.

If $\beta = \dfrac{1}{α}$,

$\alpha + \dfrac{1}{α} = {α}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{α}^{2}} = {\left(\alpha + \dfrac{1}{α}\right)}^{2} - 2$

$⇒ {\left(\alpha + \dfrac{1}{α}\right)}^{2} - \left(\alpha + \dfrac{1}{α}\right) - 2 = 0 ⇒ \alpha + \dfrac{1}{α} = 2$ or $- 1 ⇒ \alpha = 1 or \omega, {ω}^{2}$

Hence number of such equations are four $\left(0, 0\right), \left(0, 1\right), \left(1, 1\right) \left(\omega, {ω}^{2}\right)$

91917.text: A survey shows that $69%$ students like mathematics, whereas $75%$ like chemistry. If $x%$ students like both the subjects, then the maximum value of $x$ is
91917.sol:
Let, total students in survey be $100$

If mathematics is represented by $m$ & chemistry by $c$, then
$n\left(m ∩ c\right) = x$
Given, $n\left(m\right) = 69, n\left(c\right) = 75$
Now, $n\left(m ∪ c\right) = n\left(m\right) + n\left(c\right) - n\left(m ∩ c\right)$
$= 69 + 75 – x$
$= 144 – x$
$∵ 75 \le n\left(m ∪ c\right) \le 100$
$75 \le 144 - x \le 100$
$∴$ $44 \le x \le 69$

92904.text: The work function of a metal is in the range of $\text{2}\text{eV}\text{to}\text{5}\text{eV}$. Find which of the following wavelength of light cannot be used for photoelectric effect. (Consider, Planck's constant $= \text{4} \times {10}^{- \text{15}} \text{eV-s}$, velocity of light $\text{=3} \times {10}^{8}{m s}^{-1}$)
92904.sol:
Given that, $2eV \le ϕ \le 5eV$

Wavelength corresponding to minimum and maximum values of work function are

${\lambda}_\max = \dfrac{hc}{E} = \dfrac{4 \times {10}^{- 15} \times 3 \times {10}^{8}}{2}$

$= 6 \times {10}^{- 7}m = 600nm$

And ${\lambda}_\min = \dfrac{hc}{E} = \dfrac{4 \times {10}^{- 15} \times 3 \times {10}^{8}}{5}$

$= 2.4 \times {10}^{- 7}m = 240nm$

Clearly wavelength range would be $240 \le \lambda \le 600$

Thus, wavelength 650 nm is not suitable for photoelectric effect.

Growth pattern of cell, organisms is uniform under favourable conditions & a typical growth curve in plants is sigmoidal. Thus following phases of growth are recognized.

(i) Lag phase: In lag period the growth is slow. It represents formative or cell division phase.

(ii) Log phase: Also called as exponential phase. During this phase growth is maximum & most rapid. It represents cell elongation phase.

(iii) Steady or stationary phase: It represents cell maturation phase.

Time taken in growth phases (mainly log phase) is called as grand period of growth.

100701.subject: Physics
100701.text: A block of mass $4\text{ kg}$ is placed on a smooth horizontal table. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table to a hanging block of mass $1\text{ kg}$. The acceleration of the system in terms of acceleration due to gravity ($g$) is:
100701.sol:
Let the acceleration of the system be $a$ and the tension in the string be $T$.

For the hanging block of mass $1\text{ kg}$, the equation of motion is:
$1g - T = 1a$

For the block of mass $4\text{ kg}$ on the smooth horizontal table, the driving force is only the tension:
$T = 4a$

Adding the two equations, we get:
$1g = (1 + 4)a$
$g = 5a$
$a = \dfrac{g}{5}$

Answer: $\dfrac{g}{5}$

E_1=$\sigma$T^4 \Rightarrow 20=$\sigma($500)^4 \Rightarrow $\sigma=\frac{20}{(500)^4} .Now the $temperature of the blackbody is raised to

T_2=727^{{}^{\circ}}$\mathrm{C}=$1000 $\mathrm{~K}\therefore \quad$ Rate of heat radiation per unit area

$\begin{aligned}$E_2 & =$\sigma$T_2^4=$\frac{20}{(500)^4} \times($1000)^4 \\
& =20 $\times$2^4=320 $\mathrm{cal} \mathrmm^{-2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} .
\end{aligned}$

102237.subject: Physics
102237.text: A graph displays straight lines passing through the origin, representing the Volume ($V$) versus Mass ($m$) at STP for four different gases: $\text{O}_2$, $\text{N}_2$, $\text{He}$, and $\text{H}_2$. It is assumed that the intermolecular forces in all these gases vanish completely. The lines are labeled 1, 2, 3, and 4 in decreasing order of their slopes (i.e., line 1 is the steepest). Which of the following correctly identifies the gases corresponding to lines 1, 2, 3, and 4 respectively?
102237.sol:
According to the ideal gas equation, the volume $V$ of a gas of mass $m$ and molar mass $M$ at STP is given by:

$V = \dfrac{m}{M} \times 22.4\text{ L}$

The slope of the $V$ versus $m$ graph is $\dfrac{V}{m} = \dfrac{22.4}{M}$.

Thus, the slope is inversely proportional to the molar mass $M$. The gas with the smallest molar mass will have the steepest slope (line 1).

The molar masses of the given gases are:
$\text{H}_2 = 2\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
$\text{He} = 4\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
$\text{N}_2 = 28\text{ g mol}^{-1}$
$\text{O}_2 = 32\text{ g mol}^{-1}$

Since $M_{\text{H}_2} < M_{\text{He}} < M_{\text{N}_2} < M_{\text{O}_2}$, the order of decreasing slopes is $\text{H}_2 > \text{He} > \text{N}_2 > \text{O}_2$. Therefore, lines 1, 2, 3, and 4 correspond to $\text{H}_2$, $\text{He}$, $\text{N}_2$, and $\text{O}_2$ respectively.

Answer: $\text{H}_2$, $\text{He}$, $\text{N}_2$, $\text{O}_2$

103726.subject: Physics
103726.text: Two long straight solenoids, $S_1$ and $S_2$, are constructed such that $S_1$ has length $L$, total turns $N$, and carries a current $I$. Solenoid $S_2$ has length $2L$, total turns $3N$, and carries a current $\dfrac{I}{2}$. The ratio of the magnetic field at the centre of $S_1$ to that at the centre of $S_2$ is:
103726.sol:
The magnetic field at the centre of a long solenoid is given by $B = \mu_0 n I$, where $n = \dfrac{N}{L}$ is the number of turns per unit length.

For solenoid $S_1$:
$B_1 = \mu_0 \left(\dfrac{N}{L}\right) I$

For solenoid $S_2$:
Length $= 2L$, Total turns $= 3N$, Current $= \dfrac{I}{2}$

$B_2 = \mu_0 \left(\dfrac{3N}{2L}\right) \left(\dfrac{I}{2}\right)$

$B_2 = \dfrac{3}{4} \mu_0 \left(\dfrac{N}{L}\right) I$

Taking the ratio of $B_1$ to $B_2$:
$\dfrac{B_1}{B_2} = \dfrac{\mu_0 \left(\dfrac{N}{L}\right) I}{\dfrac{3}{4} \mu_0 \left(\dfrac{N}{L}\right) I} = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{3}{4}} = \dfrac{4}{3}$

Therefore, the ratio is $4 : 3$.

Answer: $4 : 3$

The same length is now bent more sharply to give a double loop of smaller radius. The magnetic field at the centre caused by the same is

& \therefore $\frac{B^{\prime}}{B}=$4 \Rightarrow B^{\prime}=4 B

104118.subject: Physics
104118.text: In a series $L-C-R$ circuit, the resonant angular frequency is $500 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$. The difference between the two angular frequencies at which the current amplitude is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ of its maximum value is $20 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$. If the capacitance in the circuit is $40 \ \mu\text{F}$, what are the values of inductance and resistance respectively?
104118.sol:
The resonant angular frequency is given by $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$.

Squaring both sides:
$\omega_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{LC}$

Rearranging for $L$:
$L = \dfrac{1}{\omega_0^2 C} = \dfrac{1}{(500)^2 \times 40 \times 10^{-6}}$
$L = \dfrac{1}{250000 \times 40 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{1}{10} = 0.1 \text{ H}$

The difference between the half-power frequencies is the bandwidth, which is given by $\dfrac{R}{L}$.

$\text{Bandwidth} = \dfrac{R}{L} = 20 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

Substituting the value of $L$:
$\dfrac{R}{0.1} = 20$

$R = 20 \times 0.1 = 2 \ \Omega$.

Answer: $0.1 \text{ H}$ and $2 \ \Omega$

105259.subject: Physics
105259.text: The Boolean expression for a logic circuit is given by $Y = \overline{(\bar{A} + B)} \cdot A$. Out of the four possible input combinations of $A$ and $B$, for how many combinations will the output $Y$ be $1$?
105259.sol:
Given Boolean expression: $Y = \overline{(\bar{A} + B)} \cdot A$

Using De Morgan's theorem, $\overline{(X + Y)} = \bar{X} \cdot \bar{Y}$.

Therefore, $\overline{(\bar{A} + B)} = \overline{\overline{A}} \cdot \bar{B} = A \cdot \bar{B}$

Substituting this back into the expression for $Y$:

$Y = (A \cdot \bar{B}) \cdot A$

Using the Boolean algebra rule $A \cdot A = A$:

$Y = A \cdot \bar{B}$

The output $Y = 1$ only when $A = 1$ and $\bar{B} = 1$ (which means $B = 0$).

Thus, out of the four possible input combinations $(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)$, only the combination $A = 1, B = 0$ gives $Y = 1$.

The output is $1$ for exactly $1$ combination.

Answer: $1$

106983.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
106983.text: Identify the correct statement regarding Oxygen and Sulphur:
options: Oxygen has $6$ valence orbitals and can form $d\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds.
Sulphur is restricted to a maximum covalency of four because it lacks vacant $d$-orbitals in its ground state.
Sulphur has $9$ valence orbitals and can expand its covalency to form $d\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds.
Oxygen has $4$ valence orbitals but can form $d\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds due to its exceptionally small size.
106983.sol:
Oxygen (Group 16, $n=2$) has $6$ valence electrons but only $4$ valence orbitals (one $2s$ and three $2p$). Due to the complete absence of $d$-orbitals in the second shell, it cannot expand its octet and forms only $p\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds.

Sulphur (Group 16, $n=3$) has $6$ valence electrons and $9$ valence orbitals (one $3s$, three $3p$, and five $3d$). The presence of vacant $3d$ orbitals in its valence shell allows Sulphur to expand its covalency (up to six) and form $d\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds (e.g., in $SO_2$ and $SO_3$).

Therefore, the statement regarding Sulphur having $9$ valence orbitals and forming $d\pi-p\pi$ bonds is the only correct one.

Answer: Sulphur has $9$ valence orbitals and can expand its covalency to form $d\pi-p\pi$ multiple bonds.

- Assertion (A): "Reaction of 1-butene with HBr gives 1-bromobutane as a major product." This is incorrect. According to Markovnikov's rule, the hydrogen atom of HBr adds to the carbon atom of the double bond that already has more hydrogen atoms. Thus, in the reaction of 1butene (\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}_2\)) with HBr, the hydrogen adds to \(\mathrm{CH}_2\) and the bromine adds to the second carbon atom (\(C H\)) to give 2-bromobutane as the major product.
- Reason (R): "Addition of HBr to unsymmetrical alkenes proceeds according to Markovnikov's rule." This is correct. Markovnikov's rule states that for an electrophilic addition reaction of a protic acid (like HBr) to an unsymmetrical alkene, the proton adds to the carbon with more hydrogen atoms, and the halide adds to the more substituted carbon.
The assertion is incorrect, but the reason is correct. Therefore, the answer is (4) (A) is not correct but (R) is correct.

119293.subject: Chemistry
119293.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): An unknown compound ($\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}$) that forms a 2,4-DNP derivative but fails to reduce Fehling's solution must definitively be a ketone.

Reason (R): Aromatic aldehydes do not reduce Fehling's solution.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
119293.sol:
Assertion (A) states that a compound with formula $\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}$ giving a positive 2,4-DNP test but a negative Fehling's test must definitively be a ketone.

While ketones do give a positive 2,4-DNP test and a negative Fehling's test, aromatic aldehydes also exhibit the exact same behavior.

For the formula $\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}$, the compound could be a ketone like acetophenone ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$) or an aromatic aldehyde like o-, m-, or p-tolualdehyde ($\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{CHO}$).

Therefore, it cannot be definitively concluded that the compound is a ketone. Assertion (A) is false.

Reason (R) states that aromatic aldehydes do not reduce Fehling's solution. This is a factual statement as mild oxidizing agents like Fehling's solution cannot oxidize aromatic aldehydes (unlike aliphatic aldehydes). Reason (R) is true.

Hence, Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

Answer: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true

119302.subject: Chemistry
119302.text: Compound P ($\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}$) gives a red orange precipitate with $2,4$-DNP reagent and it does not reduce Fehling's reagent. On drastic oxidation with chromic acid, P gives an aromatic product Q that produces effervescence on treating with aq. $\text{NaHCO}_3$. Compounds P and Q, respectively, are :
119302.sol:
Compound P ($\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}$) gives a red-orange precipitate with $2,4$-DNP reagent, indicating the presence of a carbonyl group.

P does not reduce Fehling's reagent, which implies it is either a ketone or an aromatic aldehyde.

The requirement of "drastic oxidation" strongly suggests that P is a ketone. Ketones resist mild oxidation and require drastic conditions (such as chromic acid) to undergo C-C bond cleavage, whereas aldehydes are easily oxidized.

Acetophenone ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$) is a ketone that fits the molecular formula $\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}$.

Drastic oxidation of acetophenone with chromic acid cleaves the methyl group to yield benzoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$), which is compound Q.

Benzoic acid is an aromatic carboxylic acid that reacts with aqueous $\text{NaHCO}_3$ to produce effervescence of $\text{CO}_2$ gas.

Therefore, P is acetophenone and Q is benzoic acid.

Answer: 4

Based on the given characteristics (elongated marine vertebrate, ectoparasite on fishes, cartilaginous skeleton, closed circulation), animal 'X' belongs to Class Cyclostomata.

122725.text: What type of phyllotaxy is observed when more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl?
122725.sol: Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch. This is usually of three types – alternate, opposite and whorled (Figure 5.6). In alternate type of phyllotaxy, a single leaf arises at each node in alternate manner, as in china rose, mustard and sun flower plants. In opposite type, a pair of leaves arise at each node and lie opposite to each other as in Calotropis and guava plants. If more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl, it is called whorled, as in Alstonia.
